title: No compulsion, still
tomorrow: a friend's question turns into an argument. stay or walk away?

cards: Somebody discovers a podcast, a diet, a running app, and suddenly every conversation bends toward it. Friends start answering their texts a little slower.
So when someone is curious about what you love, how much do you share? The Qur'an's answer sits in a strange spot.
Just before it comes the passage known as the Throne Verse: a God who never tires and never sleeps, whose throne takes in the heavens and the earth. Power, as big as the book describes it.
And the very next line says: "There is no compulsion in religion." Why put that there?

teach.b: Read on and the puzzle starts to solve itself. In Pickthall's words: "The right direction is henceforth distinct from error." The case has been made, clearly.
Power that big doesn't need a headlock; the choice is left with the person. A report in Sunan Abu Dawud gives the verse a human setting.
Some families in Medina had children who had grown up among a Jewish tribe of the city, and when that tribe had to leave Medina, the parents said they would not let their children go.
The verse came: no compulsion in religion.
Not even, the report suggests, for your own child.
The Qur'an says the same to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself: he is there to remind, it says, not to stand guard over anyone.

And it gives the method: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." So sharing is welcome: wisdom, beauty, a good reason, offered when someone's asking.
What it can't become is pressure. The tenth link.
The guilt trip. The friendship that only exists for the pitch. One for tonight: the Qur'an's line against forcing anyone sits right after its picture of God holding up the heavens.

how: Muslims share their faith through what the Qur'an calls wisdom and fair exhortation: answering when asked, inviting friends to an iftar or an open mosque day, and leaving the choice with the listener.

o: belief can't be forced, so sharing stays an offer
only adults may choose a religion for themselves
faith is private, so it's best never discussed

games.q: the verse and its neighbors — tap the pairs.
p: God who never sleeps or tires

s: 'no compulsion' means Muslims shouldn't talk about their faith
the Qur'an also says to call with wisdom and fair exhortation. sharing is welcome; forcing isn't.
2:256 comes right after the Throne Verse
2:255 describes God's power; the next line says no compulsion in religion.
a report ties the verse to parents and their own children
in Sunan Abu Dawud, Medinan parents wanted to keep their children; the verse said no compulsion.

games.q: at a party, a classmate asks why you're not drinking. you have a whole speech ready about it. what fits 'share, don't push'?
o: give the full speech. she asked, so she wants all of it.
give one short, honest reason, and let her ask more if she wants.
dodge with 'i'm driving'. faith is private, so keep it out.
games.why: the Qur'an's method is wisdom and fair exhortation, and 2:256 leaves the choice with the listener. a short true answer is an offer; the speech turns into a push, and the dodge shares nothing.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up: something held out, nothing gripped. Keep them open for the whole sit. If someone you'd love to share your faith with comes to mind, keep the hands open toward them too.
